Not even malicious. Just... collateral. Leon stared up at his cuffed wrist. The skin was already red, edges ringed with angry indentations. The others had no idea. Oh God. Every single time they passed through in chase... it would happen again . They would have no choice but to keep coming back. And he would have no choice but to keep taking it. “.... Shit.” Chapter 2: Short Circuit Jake crouched low behind a cracked vinyl privacy screen, its peeling edge pressed against his shoulder as he tried to stay perfectly still. The footsteps were close — not quite sprinting, but fast enough to signal active chase. Somewhere nearby, a generator had blown — he’d heard it not long ago, a sharp burst and the whine of overtaxed wires. The hallway had lit briefly with the hum of a static surge. A wide-area pulse. The jolt had dropped him into a dream of white noise and warped faces — the floor writhing beneath him like something alive, muscles twitching out of sequence for minutes after. He’d woken up behind a generator he didn’t remember fixing, pulse hammering in time with a memory he couldn’t name. He wasn’t keen on doing that again anytime soon. He pressed one hand to the floor to steady himself, heart beating too loud in his ears. He felt it in his teeth before he felt it in his skin — the telltale buzz of an incoming shock. It gathered pressure like a weather front, a phantom weight that prickled across the back of his neck and tightened the tendons in his forearms. It felt fainter than the last few times he had been shocked today. Hopefully, he was far enough out of range to not get more than a passing numbness this time. It was never overly debilitating, but the random hallucinations and muscle twinges were something he could really do without. He flexed his fingers, checking for tremors. Still there — faint, but present. Just enough to make clipping a wire a pain in the ass. “Just once,” he muttered to himself, “I’d like to have a normal goddamn trial without getting brain-fried before I even find a teammate.” From somewhere down the hall came a startled cry — high-pitched, unmistakably Meg — and Jake tensed, waiting for the telltale thud of a hit or the snap of a pallet drop. Either one would let him know what direction they were looping in so he wouldn’t have to come out of hiding so soon. No point getting zapped for a moral support cameo. He’d seen her tank worse hits and walk it off. And if it was just a standard burst, she’d be fine. Shaken, maybe, but still mobile. The air buzzed again with a second charge building. Jake barely had time to suck in a breath before something new reached his ears — a voice, muffled, but urgent enough to raise every hair on his neck. "Wait - DON’T..." The shockwave rippled through the air, a low static buzz that flared briefly across the space. A single spark cracked off the edge of the privacy screen, catching Jake on the arm. He let out a sharp hiss, jerking away from the contact. “Damn it—” he muttered, rubbing the angry red mark where the spark had connected with skin. The scream that followed made him pause in confusion. It had layers — a secondary pitch, deeper, more ragged. Not fear. Not panic. Just raw pain. Jake’s brow furrowed. That wasn’t Meg. Someone else had gotten caught in the blast. If he didn’t know better, he’d think someone got hit trying to talk Herman down or something. Unless you were right up against it, the shocks only messed with your mind and nerves. They didn’t really hurt . For someone to sound like they were in that much pain from a static blast, they would have needed to be practically touching the Doctor. Who else was with them, anyways? He remembered Herman carrying someone when he’d pulled that earlier sabotage, but hadn’t gotten a good look. Whoever it was hadn’t been screaming at the time — just flailing — so he’d assumed they’d sort themselves out or recover once the hook was back. Regardless, it would have been a stupid move, really. The Doctor wasn’t one of the killers who could be reasoned with. He took his job seriously and with a delight that bordered on mania some days. But that second scream — that yelp — landed wrong. It didn’t echo forward. It set the hairs on the back of Jake’s neck prickling, an unease sitting heavy in his stomach. It had sounded like it came from behind the wall at his back. The room at his back didn’t have a generator in it. No totem. No chest. Nothing useful. Just junk furniture, broken trays, the kind of clutter the Fog dumped in rooms to fill space. He’d passed through it earlier with barely a glance. It wasn’t even a particularly good hiding spot. So why the hell would anyone be in there? Did something get added in that he missed? The chaos outside eventually pulled away, the chase bleeding into another corner of the complex. Jake stood slowly, ears straining, and caught the tail end of a broken voice, exhausted and angry, from behind the wall. “Fucking hell. Can I just — breathe — for two seconds?” Jake’s brow furrowed. He placed a palm against the cool tile, tracing his way silently around the corner until he reached the doorframe of the adjacent room. Eyes scanning instinctively. Still no objectives.
